PS) aims to train a model on datasets distributed across the nodes of a graph, a paradigm best represented by Federated Learning (FL). A primary hurdle in FL is the communication overhead between the server and the nodes, often alleviated in practice by performing multiple local updates per iteration before synchronization. However, the non-i.i.d., or statistically diverse, nature of the node data frequently results in biased models and slow convergence rates where traditional FL iterations struggle to overcome. To mitigate communication costs while preserving the statistical properties of the nodes' data, we introduce a novel, fully decentralized framework known as Heterogeneous Device Learning (HDL). In HDL, the distribution of updates received from the nodes is regulated not merely by the updates themselves, but also by an easily calculable, per-node time-dependent weighting function. During each iteration, nodes that more rapidly generate updates calculate their contributions with proportionally higher weights to calculate the global model. Furthermore, to further reduce overhead, HDL employs a permutation-based selection strategy for active nodes and proposes calculable policies to choose those most likely to minimize the bias introduced by data heterogeneity. Collectively, these innovations constitute the HDL framework. Extensive simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate that HDL significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art FL techniques, delivering substantial global model accuracy improvements and global convergence gains.
